You can establish a routine by aiming for 7-9 hours of quality sleep each night. A consistent sleep schedule helps regulate immune system functions and repair the body.

By engaging in activities like meditation, deep breathing exercises, or hobbies you enjoy, you can practice stress-relieving techniques. Chronic stress can weaken your immune system, so finding ways to manage it is key.

By regularly washing your hands with soap and water, you can prevent the spread of germs and infections.

posts.title: Protein vs. Amino Acids: What's the Difference and Do You Need Both?
posts.excerpt: This article was written in collaboration with Bare Aminos. Over the last two weeks, we've built the case: muscle is your metabolism's best friend, protecting it during weight loss is non-negotiable.
posts.body:
This article was written in collaboration with Bare Aminos.

Over the last two weeks, we’ve built the case: muscle is your metabolism’s best friend, protecting it during weight loss is non-negotiable, and hitting your protein target on a suppressed appetite is genuinely hard.

Which brings us to the question we hear most often: What’s the difference between protein and amino acids, and if I take one, do I need the other?

Table of Contents

  • Understanding the Relationship Between Protein and Amino Acids
  • Why This Matters More on a GLP-1
  • So, Do You Need Both?
  • Where Bare Aminos Fits
  • The Takeaway

Understanding the Relationship Between Protein and Amino Acids

Every protein you eat, whether it’s chicken, eggs, yoghurt or a shake, is a long chain of amino acids. When you eat it, your digestive system spends hours breaking that chain apart because your body can’t use protein in its whole form. It can only use the amino acids inside.

Of the 20 amino acids, nine are essential. Your body cannot make them, so they must come from food. Among those nine, leucine plays a particularly important role. When enough leucine arrives at once, it switches on the process researchers call muscle protein synthesis, signalling your body to repair and maintain muscle.

Protein is the delivery vehicle. Essential amino acids are the cargo. Leucine is the ignition key.

Why This Matters More on a GLP-1

For someone eating three balanced meals with plenty of protein, the distinction between protein and amino acids is mostly academic. Either way, the amino acids reach the body.

On a medically-guided weight-loss programme, three things change.

  • Appetite is lower. Appetite suppression means less food, which means fewer amino acids arriving at the very time your body needs them to protect muscle during a significant calorie deficit.
  • Digestion is slower. These medications deliberately slow gastric emptying. A large protein meal sits in the stomach for longer and takes more time to break down, which is one reason rich meals and thick protein shakes can feel overwhelming.
  • Muscle is under greater pressure. A meaningful share of rapid weight loss can come from lean mass, so the muscle repair signal needs to be activated consistently, not only on the occasions when you manage a large protein-rich meal.

Essential amino acids (EAAs) offer a different approach. They are the amino acids themselves rather than complete proteins, so they don’t need to be broken down first. 

They are rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream and can trigger muscle protein synthesis from a light, clear drink that contains very few calories and places very little demand on digestion. Research from the International Society of Sports Nutrition supports free-form EAAs as an effective and gram-for-gram highly efficient way to stimulate muscle protein synthesis.

So, Do You Need Both?

Yes, because they serve different purposes.

Food protein remains the foundation. It provides volume, satiety, micronutrients and the full spectrum of amino acids. Nothing replaces it, and the food-first strategies discussed last week still apply.

EAAs are a targeted addition for the days when appetite won’t cooperate, after training sessions or during long gaps between small meals. A low-volume serving provides the essential amino acids, including a meaningful amount of leucine, without asking much of your appetite.

Think of it this way: food protein supplies the building materials. EAAs help keep the construction going when you’re struggling to bring enough materials to the site.

Where Bare Aminos Fits

Bare Aminos is a South African-made supplement built for exactly this gap.

Each serving of Bare Aminos contains all nine essential amino acids, including 2 g of leucine, in a light, clear drink with fewer than 20 calories and no bloating.

It is designed for the days when your appetite makes hitting your protein target difficult. If you’re on a guided programme, ask your Zapmed doctor whether adding EAAs belongs in your plan. If you’d like to learn more, take the Bare quiz or explore the range.

  • RELATED POST: How to Prepare for Your First Online Doctor Consultation in South Africa

The Takeaway

Protein and amino acids aren’t competitors. Protein delivers the amino acids your body needs, while essential amino acids provide those building blocks in their most free form. Build your diet around protein-rich foods, then use EAAs strategically on the days when a suppressed appetite leaves you short. The muscle you’re protecting today is also protecting your metabolism for the future.

posts.title: How to Hit Your Proteins When Your Appetite's Gone
posts.excerpt: This article was written in collaboration with Bare Aminos. Last week we made the case that muscle is your metabolism's best friend, and that protein is one of the two levers that protect it during weight loss.
posts.body:
This article was written in collaboration with Bare Aminos.

Last week we made the case that muscle is your metabolism’s best friend, and that protein is one of the two levers that protect it during weight loss.

Here’s the problem nobody warns you about. The same quieter appetite that makes medical weight-loss treatment effective can also make eating enough protein surprisingly difficult.

When two bites feel like a meal, “just eat more chicken” is useless advice. So let’s get practical. Here’s your target, your toolkit, and what to do when food alone can’t get you there.

Your Number

For muscle preservation during weight loss, most guidance recommends around 1.2 to 1.6g of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. For an 80kg person, that’s roughly 95 to 130g of protein every day, despite an appetite that may only want a fraction of the food it once did.

For context, a palm-sized chicken breast contains about 30g of protein. Most people’s “normal” day delivers only 50 to 70g without much thought. The gap is real.

The South African Protein Toolkit

The trick with a suppressed appetite is protein density. You want the most protein per bite, so the little you feel like eating works as hard as possible. Some local favourites include:

  • Eggs (about 6 to 7g each). Soft-scrambled eggs are often easier to eat when nothing else appeals.
  • Greek yoghurt or double-cream plain yoghurt (about 9 to 10g per 100g). Cold, simple, and easy on a flat appetite.
  • Biltong (about 50g of protein per 100g). One of the most protein-dense snacks around. A few slices between meals can make a meaningful difference.
  • Chicken breast and tinned tuna (about 25 to 30g per portion). Reliable staples that are easy to shred into smaller, more manageable portions.
  • Cottage cheese (about 11g per 100g). A simple option on a Provita when a full meal feels like too much.
  • Maas or amasi (about 3 to 4g per 100g). Familiar, gentle, and easy to drink.

Three small habits often make a bigger difference than any single food. Eat your protein first, while your appetite is strongest. 

Spread your intake across the day by aiming for 25 to 30g at three or four meals, since the body uses protein more efficiently in moderate doses than in one large serving. Finally, don’t overlook liquid options such as yoghurt, maas, or smoothies. They can often get past the “I can’t face food” barrier more easily than solid meals.

When Food Alone Can’t Get You There

Here’s the honest part. Some days, even with the best toolkit, a suppressed appetite simply won’t let you eat more than 100g of protein. Force-feeding isn’t the answer. Heavy protein shakes often aren’t either. A 300ml thick, milky shake is exactly the kind of volume that a quiet appetite tends to reject. For many people, dairy-heavy whey also brings bloating.

That’s where a low-volume protein top-up can be useful. It helps support your muscles without demanding more stomach space than you have. One approach is to use essential amino acids, the part of protein your body relies on to trigger muscle repair, delivered in a light drink instead of a heavy shake.

What’s the difference between protein and amino acids, and do you actually need both? That’s exactly what we’ll cover in next week’s article, with the science made simple.

The Takeaway

Feeling less hungry is an intended effect of treatment. It also means protein becomes something you need to plan for. Know your target, start every meal with protein, lean on protein-dense foods such as biltong, and spread your intake across the day. On the days when food simply isn’t enough, remember that low-volume protein top-ups exist to help bridge the gap.

Not sure if today’s the day to reach for amino acids or push through with a boiled egg instead? That’s a call a health coach can help you make. They get to know your routine, your fridge, and your bad days, which means the advice you get is shaped around your actual life rather than a generic list of do’s and don’ts.

posts.title: Why Muscle is Your Metabolism's Best Friend
posts.excerpt: If you're losing weight, especially on a medically guided programme, the number on the scale is only half the story. The other half is what you're losing.
posts.body:
This article was written in collaboration with Bare Aminos.

If you’re losing weight, especially on a medically guided programme, the number on the scale is only half the story. The other half is what you’re losing. And the part almost nobody talks about is that some of it is muscle.

That matters more than most people realise because muscle isn’t just about strength. It’s the most metabolically expensive tissue you own and your metabolism’s best friend.

Muscle is where your metabolism lives

Every kilogram of muscle you carry burns energy around the clock — even while you sleep. Muscle tissue is a major driver of your resting metabolic rate: the energy your body spends just keeping you alive, which accounts for the majority of the calories you burn in a day.

Lose muscle, and that baseline quietly drops. The practical effect: the same eating habits that maintained your weight before now sit slightly above your new, lower burn rate.

This is one reason weight regain after rapid loss is so common. The body you end up with burns less than the body you started with.

Muscle is also your glucose sponge

Beyond burning calories, muscle is your body’s biggest disposal site for blood glucose. When you eat carbohydrates, muscle is where much of it should go. More muscle means better blood-sugar control and insulin sensitivity — which is exactly what most weight-loss journeys are trying to improve in the first place.

The catch with rapid weight loss

When you lose weight quickly, your body doesn’t only draw on fat. Research on modern weight-loss medication shows that a meaningful share of the total weight lost can be lean mass — in some studies, a figure in the region of 25–40% of what’s lost. (Lean mass isn’t all muscle, but muscle makes up a large part of it.)

That’s not a reason to avoid effective treatment. It’s a reason to be deliberate about protecting muscle while you lose so that the weight you lose is overwhelmingly the weight you wanted gone.

The two levers that protect muscle

The good news: protecting muscle during weight loss is well understood, and it comes down to two things you control.

1. Resistance training — the signal. Muscle is retained when it’s used. 

Two to three short resistance-training sessions a week — using weights, resistance bands, or body weight — tells your body, unambiguously, that this tissue is needed. Walking is wonderful, but it doesn’t send this particular signal.

2. Protein — the raw material. Your body can’t maintain muscle without the building blocks to repair it. During weight loss, protein requirements increase, not decrease. Most guidance for preserving lean mass sits around 1.2–1.6g of protein per kilogram of body weight per day, meaningfully more than most people typically eat.

And there’s the rub: the same appetite suppression that makes weight loss possible makes eating enough protein genuinely difficult. That’s the challenge we’ll unpack in our next article, with practical, South African-kitchen ways to solve it.

The takeaway

Weight loss done well isn’t about a smaller number. It’s about a better composition. Keep the muscle, and you keep the metabolism, the strength, the blood-sugar control and the shape. Lose it, and you’ve made maintenance harder than it needs to be.

Muscle is your metabolism’s best friend. Treat it like one.

posts.title: What Causes Acne and How to Treat It Online
posts.excerpt: Acne is one of the most common skin conditions, affecting teenagers and adults alike. While many people expect breakouts to disappear after their teenage years, acne often continues well into adulthood.
posts.body:
Acne is one of the most common skin conditions, affecting teenagers and adults alike. While many people expect breakouts to disappear after their teenage years, acne often continues well into adulthood or appears for the first time later in life.

Living with acne can affect far more than your skin. Persistent spots, painful cysts, and marks left behind after breakouts can influence confidence, social interactions, and even professional life. The good news is that effective treatment is available, and you no longer need to spend hours waiting for appointments to begin improving your skin.

Understanding why acne develops is the first step towards choosing the right treatment.

What causes acne?

Acne develops when hair follicles become blocked with excess oil, dead skin cells, and bacteria. Several factors usually work together, which is why there is rarely a single cause.

Your skin naturally produces an oily substance called sebum. Sebum helps keep the skin healthy and prevents it from becoming too dry. Problems begin when too much sebum combines with dead skin cells, creating a blockage inside the pore.

Once a pore is blocked, bacteria that naturally live on the skin can multiply. Your body’s immune system reacts to the bacteria, leading to redness, swelling, and the familiar appearance of pimples.

Different people produce different amounts of oil, which explains why some people rarely experience acne while others struggle with ongoing breakouts.

Hormones play a major role

Hormonal changes are among the biggest contributors to acne.

During puberty, hormone levels increase significantly, stimulating the oil glands to produce more sebum. This explains why acne is so common during the teenage years.

Hormonal fluctuations can also affect adults. Many women notice breakouts before their menstrual cycle, during pregnancy, or around menopause. Conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome can also contribute to persistent acne because they influence hormone levels.

Hormonal acne often appears around the chin, jawline, and lower face, although it can develop anywhere on the body.

Does diet cause acne?

Diet is not the sole cause of acne, but growing evidence suggests that certain foods may contribute to breakouts in some people.

Foods with a high glycaemic index, including sugary snacks, white bread, and sweetened drinks, may increase inflammation and stimulate hormones linked to oil production.

Some studies have also found a possible connection between dairy products and acne in certain individuals. This does not mean everyone should stop consuming dairy, but it may be worth paying attention to how your skin responds.

Eating a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit, lean protein, and whole grains supports overall skin health, even if it does not completely prevent acne.

Stress and acne

Stress does not directly cause acne, but it can make existing breakouts worse.

When you are under pressure, your body releases hormones that can increase oil production and inflammation. Stress may also affect sleep, eating habits, and skincare routines, all of which can influence your skin.

Finding healthy ways to manage stress can form part of a broader acne treatment plan.

Can skincare products make acne worse?

Some skincare and cosmetic products can block pores, particularly if they are heavy or oil based.

Choosing products labelled as non comedogenic means they are less likely to clog pores. Gentle cleansing twice a day is usually enough for most people. Washing too often or using harsh scrubs can irritate the skin and make acne appear more inflamed.

Picking or squeezing spots can also increase inflammation and raise the risk of permanent scarring.

Different types of acne

Not every breakout looks the same. Understanding the type of acne you have helps determine the most suitable treatment.

Whiteheads are closed blocked pores that appear as small white bumps.

Blackheads are open blocked pores where the trapped material darkens after exposure to air.

Papules are small red bumps that become inflamed.

Pustules contain pus and often have a white or yellow centre.

Nodules develop deeper beneath the skin and are usually painful.

Cysts are larger inflamed lesions that carry the greatest risk of scarring and often require prescription treatment.

How is acne treated?

Acne treatment depends on the severity of your acne, how long you have had it, and whether previous treatments have worked.

Mild acne often responds well to topical treatments that reduce bacteria, unclog pores, and control inflammation. Ingredients such as benzoyl peroxide and retinoids are commonly used for this purpose.

Moderate acne may require prescription creams or oral medication to reduce inflammation and control bacterial growth.

More severe acne, particularly painful cystic acne, often needs stronger prescription medication under medical supervision. Early treatment is important because ongoing inflammation increases the likelihood of permanent scarring.

Improvement rarely happens overnight. Most acne treatments take several weeks before noticeable changes appear, so consistency is essential.

Common mistakes that delay improvement

Many people become discouraged when they do not see immediate results. As a result, they frequently switch products or stop treatment too soon.

Using too many active ingredients at once can irritate the skin without improving acne more quickly.

Another common mistake is skipping moisturiser. Even oily skin needs hydration, particularly when using prescription acne treatments that may cause dryness.

Applying sunscreen every day is equally important, as some acne medications make the skin more sensitive to sunlight.

Following a treatment plan consistently gives your skin the best opportunity to improve.

When should you seek professional help?

If over the counter products have not improved your skin after several months, it may be time to seek medical advice.

You should also speak to a healthcare professional if your acne is painful, leaves scars, causes significant emotional distress, or continues returning despite your efforts.

Professional treatment can often prevent acne from becoming more severe and reduce the chance of lasting skin damage.

posts.title: Signs of Low Testosterone in South African Men
posts.excerpt: You wake up tired even after eight hours of sleep. Your motivation feels flat, your gym sessions aren't hitting the same, and your mood has been all over the place lately.
posts.body:
You wake up tired even after eight hours of sleep. Your motivation feels flat, your gym sessions aren’t hitting the same, and your mood has been all over the place lately. 

If this sounds familiar, you’re not imagining things, and you’re definitely not alone. A lot of South African men brush these changes off as stress, age, or just life catching up with them. But sometimes there’s something more going on beneath the surface. 

Testosterone plays a bigger role in how you feel day to day than most people realise.

Low testosterone often develops gradually, which makes early signs easy to overlook or dismiss. This post will walk you through the symptoms and help you understand what might be behind them.

Table of Contents

  • What Is Testosterone?
  • Low Testosterone Symptoms in Men
    • Reduced Sex Drive
    • Constant Tiredness
    • Erectile Dysfunction
    • Loss of Muscle Strength
    • Weight Gain Around the Middle
    • Poor Sleep
    • Mood Changes 
  • Causes of Low Testosterone
  • Could Something Else Explain These Symptoms?
  • How is Low Testosterone Diagnosed?
    • Treatment for Low Testosterone
  • Treating the Underlying Cause
  • How Zapmed Supports Men Through This Journey

What Is Testosterone?

Testosterone is a hormone made mainly in the testicles. Every man needs healthy testosterone levels for normal body function throughout adulthood.

Healthy testosterone levels support muscle strength, bone health, energy, sex drive, sperm production, and emotional wellbeing. Hormone levels rise during puberty before reaching their highest point in early adulthood. A gradual decline often comes with age, although some men experience a much larger drop because of medical conditions or lifestyle factors.

Low testosterone, also known as testosterone deficiency or male hypogonadism, develops when hormone levels fall below the normal range and symptoms begin to appear. A blood test, together with a medical assessment, helps confirm the diagnosis.

Low Testosterone Symptoms in Men

Reduced Sex Drive

Low libido is one of the most common signs of low testosterone in men. Testosterone influences sexual desire, so when levels fall, many men notice they think about sex less often, feel less interested in intimacy, or no longer have the same level of desire they once did.

Constant Tiredness

Low testosterone often leaves men with little energy from the start of the day, even after enough sleep. Daily tasks may feel harder than usual, while physical activity becomes more difficult than before.

A drop in energy can also reduce motivation for exercise, hobbies, or household responsibilities. Fatigue linked to low testosterone usually continues for weeks or months instead of disappearing after a good night’s sleep.

Erectile Dysfunction

Low testosterone does not always cause erectile dysfunction on its own, although both conditions often overlap. Many men notice fewer spontaneous erections or greater difficulty maintaining an erection.

Medical assessment helps identify the underlying cause because erectile dysfunction may also signal cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or other health concerns.

Loss of Muscle Strength

Regular exercise normally helps preserve muscle mass. Lower testosterone can make strength training feel less rewarding because muscles respond differently.

Some men notice weaker grip strength, reduced endurance or greater difficulty lifting weights that once felt comfortable. Everyday activities may also become harder over time.

Weight Gain Around the Middle

Extra body fat around the abdomen often accompanies lower testosterone levels. Higher body fat may also lower testosterone further, which creates a cycle that becomes difficult to break without the right guidance.

Healthy eating, physical activity, and medical care can help interrupt that cycle.

Poor Sleep

Sleep and testosterone share a close connection.

Interrupted sleep can lower testosterone, while low testosterone may contribute to restless nights. Some men wake frequently or struggle to feel refreshed after a full night’s sleep.

Sleep apnoea also needs to be taken into consideration, particularly among men who snore loudly or feel exhausted during the day.

Mood Changes 

Low testosterone can change emotional wellbeing as much as physical health. Some men notice irritability, low mood, reduced motivation, or a loss of enjoyment in activities they once valued. However, a hormone imbalance should never become the only explanation for emotional symptoms because depression, anxiety, poor sleep, and other medical conditions can create similar experiences.

Causes of Low Testosterone

Several medical and lifestyle factors can lower testosterone levels.

Ageing is among the most common reasons because hormone levels gradually decline over time. Obesity also contributes because excess body fat changes hormone balance throughout the body.

Type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease and certain genetic conditions may lower testosterone. Injury to the testicles, chemotherapy, radiation treatment and infections can also reduce hormone levels.

Long-term use of opioid pain medication, anabolic steroids and some prescription medicines may contribute as well.

High alcohol intake, poor sleep and untreated sleep apnoea can add further strain.

Accurate diagnosis matters because successful treatment depends on finding the underlying cause rather than focusing only on hormone levels.

Could Something Else Explain These Symptoms?

Many symptoms linked to low testosterone overlap with other health conditions. Poor sleep, depression, thyroid disorders, nutritional deficiencies and certain medications can all produce similar changes.

A diagnosis therefore depends on more than symptoms alone. Blood tests, medical history and a discussion about your overall health help build a complete picture.

Self-diagnosis often leads men in the wrong direction. Professional medical advice helps identify the real cause and guides appropriate treatment.

How is Low Testosterone Diagnosed?

Diagnosis involves more than a simple checklist of symptoms.

Doctors usually request a morning blood test because testosterone levels are highest earlier in the day. More than one test may be necessary, especially if the first result falls close to the lower end of the normal range.

Additional blood tests may help identify the cause of lower testosterone or rule out other conditions that produce similar symptoms.

Treatment for Low Testosterone

For men with confirmed low testosterone and related symptoms, testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) is the most common treatment. It is available in several forms, including:

  • Testosterone injections, given every 1 to 12 weeks depending on the formulation.
  • Testosterone gels, applied to the skin daily.
  • Testosterone patches, worn on the skin and changed regularly.
  • Testosterone pellets, inserted under the skin and replaced every few months.
  • Oral testosterone capsules, which may be suitable for some men.

TRT can improve:

  • Sex drive
  • Erectile function in some men
  • Energy levels
  • Mood
  • Muscle strength and mass
  • Bone density

However, treatment requires ongoing medical supervision with regular blood tests to monitor testosterone levels, red blood cell counts, and prostate health where appropriate.

Treating the Underlying Cause

Low testosterone is not always a condition on its own. Your healthcare provider may recommend treating the cause instead of, or before, starting testosterone therapy. This could include:

  • Losing excess weight if obesity is contributing to low testosterone.
  • Managing type-2 diabetes or other chronic medical conditions.
  • Improving sleep, especially if you have obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • Adjusting medications that may reduce testosterone, if medically appropriate.
  • Treating problems affecting the pituitary gland or testicles.

In some cases, testosterone levels improve once the underlying issue is addressed.

How Zapmed Supports Men Through This Journey

Excess body fat, particularly around the abdomen, can disrupt hormone balance by increasing the conversion of testosterone into oestrogen and contributing to inflammation and insulin resistance. Weight loss can help reverse some of these changes.

posts.title: The Starter's Guide to Contraceptive Pills in South Africa
posts.excerpt: Every woman who chooses a method of family planning has her own reasons for doing so. Some want to plan when to grow their family, on their own terms and in their own time.
posts.body:
Every woman who chooses a method of family planning has her own reasons for doing so. 

Some want to plan when to grow their family, on their own terms and in their own time. Others need relief from painful periods, heavy bleeding or hormonal acne. Many simply want a say over their own body and their own future. 

Whatever the reason behind that choice, it deserves respect, never judgement.

Among the many contraceptive methods available to South African women today, the pill is one of the easiest to access and one of the most trusted. Reliable, effective, and backed by decades of medical research, the pill has helped millions of women take charge of their reproductive health.

Here’s our beginner’s guide to contraceptive pills in South Africa.

What are Contraceptive Pills?

Contraceptive pills are tablets taken by mouth to prevent pregnancy. They contain hormones that stop ovulation, thicken cervical mucus, and thin the lining of the uterus, three barriers that together make pregnancy far less likely.

Types of Contraceptive Pills in South Africa

South African women generally have two main pill types to choose between: the combined pill and the progestogen-only pill.

The combined pill contains two hormones, oestrogen and progestogen, and works by stopping ovulation each month. Most brands available locally fall into this category, and doctors often start new patients on a low-dose combined pill unless there’s a medical reason to avoid oestrogen, such as migraines with aura, high blood pressure or a history of blood clots.

The progestogen-only pill, sometimes called the mini pill, contains no oestrogen at all. Doctors often recommend it to breastfeeding mothers, smokers over 35, and women who cannot take oestrogen for health reasons. Because it relies on a single hormone, timing matters more, and the pill needs to be taken within the same three-hour window each day to remain effective.

A doctor can advise on the right type based on medical history, lifestyle and any other medication a woman already takes. No single pill works best for every woman, which is exactly why a proper consultation is needed before any prescription is written.

How the Contraceptive Pill Works

Hormones in the pill send a message to the brain and ovaries that pregnancy hormones are already present, so the ovaries pause their usual monthly release of an egg. Without an egg to fertilise, pregnancy cannot happen. 

Alongside this, the pill thickens the mucus at the entrance of the cervix, which makes it much harder for sperm to travel through, and it also thins the lining of the uterus, so that even if an egg were somehow released and fertilised, implantation becomes far less likely. Taken correctly and on schedule, both types reach effectiveness above 99%.

When to Start the Pill

Timing depends on your menstrual cycle and your doctor’s advice.

Most doctors recommend beginning the combined pill on the first day of a menstrual period, since protection against pregnancy applies almost immediately. Some women prefer a Sunday start, where the first pill is swallowed on the first Sunday after a period begins, though a backup method such as condoms is wise for the first seven days with this approach.

A quick-start method also exists, where a woman begins the pill on any day of her cycle, as long as pregnancy has been ruled out beforehand. A doctor can advise on the safest starting point based on individual health history and lifestyle.

What to Do If You Miss a Pill

Busy schedules, travel, late nights, and changing routines can all lead to the occasional missed tablet.

For the combined pill, if you’re less than 24 hours late, simply take the missed pill as soon as you remember and continue as normal, no backup contraception needed. If more than 24 hours have passed, take the most recent missed pill immediately, carry on with the rest of the pack, and use condoms for the next seven days. If you missed pills during the final week of active tablets, skip the placebo week and start a new pack straight away to avoid an extended hormone-free gap.

For the progestogen-only pill, the window is far tighter. Being more than three hours late counts as a missed pill, and you’ll need backup contraception for two full days after taking your next dose.

If a missed pill coincided with unprotected sex, speak to a doctor about emergency contraception as soon as possible, since timing affects how well it works.

Possible Side Effects

Most women adjust to the pill within the first two or three months, though some mild effects are common early on. These may include nausea, headaches, breast tenderness, mild mood changes and irregular spotting between periods. Such effects usually settle as your body adapts to the new hormone levels.

Less common but more serious effects can include blood clots, high blood pressure and, in rare cases, liver problems. Women who smoke, have a history of blood clots, or carry certain other risk factors should discuss these carefully with a doctor before beginning any hormonal contraceptive.

Persistent severe headaches, chest pain, leg swelling or vision changes warrant immediate medical attention, as these can signal rare but serious complications.

Contraceptive Pill Price in South Africa

Contraceptive pills are not available without a prescription, so the initial cost includes both the doctor’s consultation and the prescribed medication.

Traditional healthcare often requires separate payments for the consultation, prescription and pharmacy collection.

Medical Aid members can access the service from R220 per month, depending on their cover.

One monthly payment removes the need to organise multiple appointments or pharmacy visits, making contraception easier to manage.

Why Choose Zapmed for Birth Control?

Zapmed connects you with qualified South African doctors through an online consultation, giving you the opportunity to discuss your health in a comfortable, judgement free space. Every prescription follows an individual medical assessment, making sure your treatment reflects your personal healthcare needs.

Frequently Asked Questions Before You Start

Can the pill affect my long term fertility?

No. Fertility returns to its normal pattern soon after you stop, for most women within a cycle or two.

Does the pill protect against sexually transmitted infections?

No. Condoms remain the only method that reduces the risk of STIs alongside pregnancy prevention, so many women pair the two methods.

Can I change to another pill?

Yes. A doctor may recommend another formulation if side effects become troublesome or your healthcare needs change over time.

Can I use the pill alongside other medication?

Certain antibiotics and epilepsy medications can reduce the pill’s effectiveness, so always mention every medication you take during your consultation.

posts.title: Can Your Relaxing Bubble Bath Secretly Cause Thrush?
posts.excerpt: A warm bubble bath feels like the perfect way to unwind, and most of us do not think twice about the products we pour in. But if you have noticed itching, irritation or unusual discharge after a soak, your bath routine may be worth a second look.
posts.body:
A warm bubble bath feels like the perfect way to unwind, and most of us do not think twice about the products we pour in. But if you have noticed itching, irritation or unusual discharge after a soak, your bath routine may be worth a second look. Thrush from bubble baths is more common than many people realise, and understanding why it happens can save you a great deal of discomfort.

What Is Vaginal Thrush?

Vaginal thrush is caused by an overgrowth of a yeast called Candida albicans. This yeast lives naturally in and on the body without causing any problems most of the time. 

It is only when the delicate balance of bacteria and yeast in the vaginal environment is disturbed that Candida multiplies beyond its usual levels and symptoms appear.

Those symptoms tend to include itching and soreness around the vulva and vagina, a thick white discharge that is often described as cottage cheese-like in texture, and sometimes a burning sensation, particularly during urination or sex. 

Thrush is not a sexually transmitted infection, and it is extremely common. Most women will experience it at least once in their lives, many far more often than that.

How Bubble Baths Can Trigger Thrush

The vagina maintains its own carefully balanced environment, slightly acidic by nature, which helps keep Candida and harmful bacteria in check. 

Bubble baths, bath bombs, and heavily fragranced soaps can disrupt this balance in several ways.

Most commercial bubble baths are a mixture of surfactants, fragrances, preservatives, and colourants. Elsewhere on the body, these ingredients are generally tolerated well. The vaginal area is a different matter.

Sitting in a bubble bath means the surrounding water, along with everything dissolved in it, comes into direct and prolonged contact with the vulva. Fragrances and surfactants in particular are known to irritate sensitive tissue, strip away the skin’s natural protective oils, and alter the vaginal pH. Once that pH shifts, the bacterial balance that keeps Candida in check is compromised. The yeast, finding conditions more to its liking, begins to proliferate.

This is why thrush after bubble baths is more common than many women realise. It is not bathing itself that causes the problem. Plain warm water poses no threat. The issue lies with what is added to it, especially products that foam heavily or carry strong synthetic fragrances.

Who Is More Susceptible?

Some women find that thrush after bubble baths becomes a recurring issue while others seem unaffected. 

This comes down to individual differences in skin sensitivity, vaginal microbiome composition, and other underlying factors.

Women who take antibiotics regularly may find themselves more vulnerable, since antibiotics reduce the good bacteria that normally keep Candida in balance.

Hormonal fluctuations throughout the menstrual cycle, during pregnancy, or around the menopause can also affect the vaginal environment in ways that make thrush more likely. 

People living with diabetes or those with a weakened immune system tend to experience thrush more frequently too.

If you keep getting thrush and you regularly enjoy bubble baths, it is worth considering whether the two might be connected for you specifically.

Simple Steps to Protect Vaginal Health

Switch to plain water for bathing around the vulval area, or to use a fragrance-free, unperfumed wash that is specifically formulated for intimate skin. 

Even if you love a bubble bath, avoiding submerging the vulva in the soapy water and rinsing thoroughly afterwards can reduce the irritant load.

Choosing shower gels and body washes without added fragrance for your general routine also helps, as does wearing breathable cotton underwear and avoiding very tight clothing that traps warmth and moisture close to the skin.

After a bath or shower, patting the area dry rather than leaving it damp matters more than people often realise. Yeast thrives in warm, moist conditions, so keeping the area dry is a simple but effective habit.

It is also worth checking the ingredients of any bath products you use regularly. If a product contains sodium lauryl sulphate, artificial fragrance, or colourants high up on the ingredients list, that is a signal it may be aggravating things.

When to Seek Treatment

Thrush responds well to treatment, but it is important to be certain that what you are experiencing is actually thrush and not something else. Bacterial vaginosis, for instance, shares some similarities but requires different treatment entirely. 

If your symptoms are new and mild, and you have had thrush before and recognise what it feels like, an over-the-counter antifungal treatment from your pharmacist may be appropriate. 

These are available as pessaries, creams or oral capsules.

However, if your symptoms are severe, if they are not improving after treatment, if this is your first time experiencing them, or if you have recurrent episodes (four or more in a year), it is worth speaking to a doctor. 

There may be an underlying reason for recurrent thrush that needs to be identified and addressed, and using antifungal treatments repeatedly without guidance is not always the right approach.

posts.body:
Few health concerns send people down an internet rabbit hole quite like finding an unfamiliar bump in an intimate area.

You look once, then again. You tell yourself it is probably nothing. A few days later, you check again. Before long, you’re comparing photographs online, reading articles and trying to work out whether what you’re seeing matches what everyone else seems to be describing.

Genital warts are often discovered this way.

Not because they cause severe symptoms or make people feel unwell, but because they raise questions. What is it? How did it get there? Does it need treatment? Do I need to see a doctor?

The first thing to know is that genital warts are common. The second is that they are not always easy to identify without professional advice. They can look different from person to person, and what seems obvious in hindsight often feels anything but obvious when you’re trying to figure it out on your own.

What Causes Genital Warts?

Genital warts are caused by certain types of the human papillomavirus, commonly known as HPV. HPV is extremely common and is spread through intimate skin to skin contact.

One of the reasons genital warts can feel confusing is that they do not always appear soon after exposure. Some people notice symptoms within weeks, while others may not develop visible warts until much later. In many cases, people carry HPV without ever developing noticeable signs.

Finding out that you have genital warts does not mean you have done anything wrong. HPV is one of the most common viruses affecting sexually active adults, which is why genital warts treatment is something doctors deal with regularly.

What Do Genital Warts Look Like?

Many people expect genital warts to be obvious, but that is not always the case.

Some appear as tiny flesh coloured bumps that are easy to miss. Others form small clusters that stand out more clearly. They may be smooth, slightly raised or have a textured appearance. In some cases, several small growths sit close together, creating a pattern that looks different from the surrounding skin.

This is why self diagnosis can be difficult. Conditions such as skin tags, harmless skin changes and other infections can sometimes look surprisingly similar.

Photographs found online can be useful for general information, but they cannot tell you with certainty what is causing your symptoms.

Where Do Genital Warts Appear?

Genital warts can appear on different parts of the genital and surrounding areas.

For women, they may develop on the vulva, around the vaginal opening, around the anus or in areas that are not easily visible without examination.

For men, they may appear on the penis, scrotum, groin or around the anus.

The location, size and number of warts all help determine the most appropriate genital warts treatment.

How Is Genital Warts Treatment Decided?

The first step is confirming that the growths are genital warts.

That may sound obvious, but a range of skin conditions can look similar at first glance. Skin tags, harmless skin growths and other dermatological conditions can sometimes be mistaken for genital warts.

Once a doctor has assessed the affected area, they can recommend the most suitable genital warts treatment based on the appearance and location of the warts.

In many cases, genital warts treatment involves prescription medication that is applied directly to the affected area. These treatments work by helping the body remove the visible warts over time.

Some people respond well to topical treatments that can be used at home, while others may require a different approach depending on the nature of the warts.

The important thing to remember is that treatment is not chosen from a menu. It is selected based on what the doctor sees during the assessment.

How Online Genital Warts Treatment Works

Not everyone feels comfortable attending a clinic for intimate health concerns.

Some people have demanding schedules. Others live far from a healthcare provider. For many, privacy is the deciding factor.

If genital warts treatment is appropriate, a prescription can be issued following the consultation. Your medication can then be arranged through a pharmacy and delivered directly to your home in discreet packaging.

The entire process takes place without the need to travel or spend time in a waiting room.

What Does Genital Warts Treatment Cost?

For those paying cash, a once off treatment option is available from R630. This includes the doctor’s consultation fee, medication and medication delivery.

The aim is to make genital warts treatment accessible without requiring multiple appointments, separate prescriptions and additional trips to the pharmacy.

Looking After Yourself During Treatment

Aftercare plays an important role in the treatment process.

Keeping the affected area clean and dry can help support healing. It is also important to use any prescribed treatment exactly as directed, even if improvement begins sooner than expected.

Avoid picking, scratching or attempting to remove warts yourself. This can irritate the skin and may make the situation worse.

If you have any concerns during treatment, or if symptoms change unexpectedly, it is worth checking in with your doctor rather than trying to manage the issue on your own.

Why It Is Worth Getting Checked

One of the most common reasons people delay seeking help is uncertainty.

They are not sure whether the growth is new. They are not convinced it is serious enough to warrant a consultation. They hope it will disappear on its own.

posts.body:
There are few things more frustrating than a payment notification that catches you by surprise. It is your money, you have planned for where it needs to go, and the last thing you want is confusion around a scheduled payment.

I Got an Email Saying My Account Will Be Debited in 48 Hours. My Account Is Debited on the 26th of Each Month.

The email is simply an advance notification that a debit instruction is scheduled to be processed. It does not necessarily mean that your debit date has changed.

If your subscription is set to be collected on the 26th of each month, that date remains your agreed payment date. The notification is sent ahead of time to let you know that the payment process is approaching and to give you an opportunity to ensure there are sufficient funds available or that your payment details are still correct.

Receiving this email does not mean your account will suddenly be debited two days earlier than normal. It is a reminder generated before the scheduled collection takes place.

If you believe your debit date has been changed incorrectly or you notice that your payment was processed on an unexpected date, please contact the Zapmed support team so we can investigate your account and provide an explanation.

What Happens If My Card Payment Fails?

The most common reasons include insufficient funds, expired cards, replacement cards issued by your bank, banking security checks or incorrect card information.

If your payment fails, the first step is to check that your card details are still current and that there are enough funds available in your account.

If the issue was temporary, such as a short term banking interruption or a balance that was not yet available, you may be able to retry the payment successfully once the issue has been resolved.

posts.excerpt: At Zapmed, we are focused on making wellness feel simpler, more accessible, and easier to fit into everyday life. Convenience matters to us.
posts.body:
At Zapmed, we are focused on making wellness feel simpler, more accessible, and easier to fit into everyday life. Convenience matters to us. It is one of the main reasons people choose online healthcare in the first place. 

While we are on the topic of convenience, many people wonder whether they can collect a three month supply of birth control pills at once instead of returning to the pharmacy every few weeks. It is a practical question, especially for busy schedules, travel plans, work commitments, or simply wanting fewer interruptions during the month.

But is it possible? Is it allowed? And how does it work in practice?

This is the question we recently received from one of our members:

“I wanted to find out if it is possible for me to get my contraceptives for 3 months at once?”

We welcome all queries and encourage you to keep sending them through. Questions like these help many other people who may be wondering the same thing. Now onto the issue.

Can You Get a 3-Month Supply of Birth Control?

Generally, yes.

Most oral contraceptive pills are routinely dispensed in one to three month quantities. In many cases, pharmacies are comfortable supplying a three month pack upfront, particularly when the prescription allows for it.

There are several situations where this commonly happens.

You have already been using the pill successfully for some time without problems.

The medication is available in a three month pack size.

The pharmacy follows a repeat dispensing approach for ongoing medication.

For many people, receiving a longer supply simply makes life easier. It means fewer trips to the pharmacy, less chance of missing doses because a refill was delayed, and greater continuity in your contraceptive routine.

At the same time, dispensing practices can vary between pharmacies.

Some pharmacies may only issue one month at a time even when additional repeats remain on the prescription. This may depend on internal policies, stock availability, or the pharmacist’s professional judgement.

First time users are also sometimes given a shorter initial supply. This allows the prescribing doctor and pharmacist to see how the medication suits the patient before issuing a larger quantity.

It is also important to remember that birth control pills are prescription medication. Even though they are commonly used, they still require proper medical oversight. Your doctor may occasionally want to review how you are responding to the medication, whether you are experiencing side effects, or whether your current pill remains the best option for your health needs.

How Long Does a Birth Control Prescription Last?

The duration of a contraceptive prescription depends on the doctor’s assessment and the type of script issued.

In many cases, a doctor may prescribe oral contraception with repeats that cover several months. This means you do not necessarily need a new consultation every month just to continue your medication.

For example, a doctor may prescribe:

  • One month supply with multiple repeats
  • Three month supply with repeats
  • A longer prescription period for stable long term users

The exact duration can vary depending on your medical history, age, risk factors, and whether you are newly starting contraception or continuing an existing routine.

For people who have been using the same contraceptive pill consistently and without complications, doctors are often comfortable prescribing for longer periods before requiring a renewal consultation.

However, it is important to understand that repeat prescriptions are subject to legal limits. For Schedule 2, 3, and 4 medicines, which include many commonly prescribed contraceptives, South African regulations allow repeat prescriptions to cover a maximum period of six months. This means that while your doctor may prescribe enough medication for a three month supply upfront, repeat prescriptions cannot legally extend beyond six months without a new medical assessment.

In practical terms, if you are continuing on the same contraceptive pill, you will typically need to consult with your doctor again after six months before a new prescription can be issued. These review appointments help ensure that the medication remains appropriate for your needs and allow your doctor to assess any changes in your health, side effects, or risk factors.

There are situations where a shorter review period may still be recommended. These can include:

There are situations where a shorter review period may still be recommended. These can include:

  • Starting a contraceptive for the first time
  • Experiencing side effects
  • Changes in blood pressure
  • Migraines or headaches
  • Smoking combined with certain age groups
  • Other health conditions that require closer monitoring

Even when your prescription includes repeats, it is still important to keep track of expiry dates and renewal timelines. Running out unexpectedly can interrupt your contraceptive coverage and create unnecessary stress.

A good approach is to request your renewal before your final pack is finished. This gives enough time for your doctor to review your prescription if needed and avoids last minute urgency.

At Zapmed, our doctors can assist with contraceptive reviews and ongoing prescriptions through a convenient online process, making repeat care far easier to manage.

Why Pharmacies Sometimes Limit Dispensing Quantities

Many people assume that if a prescription contains repeats, the pharmacy must automatically provide the entire quantity upfront. In practice, pharmacies may still apply certain dispensing limits.

This does not necessarily mean there is a problem with your prescription.

Pharmacies work within professional dispensing guidelines and operational considerations. A few factors can influence how much medication is supplied at once.

Stock availability is one of the most common reasons. Some contraceptive brands may temporarily have limited supply or may only arrive in smaller quantities from wholesalers.

Medical caution can also play a role. If someone is starting a new contraceptive for the first time, a pharmacist may prefer to dispense a smaller quantity initially while the patient adjusts to the medication.

Certain medical aid rules or reimbursement structures may also influence dispensing intervals. Some schemes place limits on how much chronic or repeat medication can be claimed at one time.

In other situations, the pharmacy may simply follow its own dispensing process for repeat medication.

If you would prefer a larger quantity upfront, it is perfectly reasonable to ask the pharmacist whether a three month supply can be dispensed based on your prescription. Often, the answer depends on what the script allows and what stock is available at the time.

Good communication between the patient, doctor, and pharmacist usually resolves most questions quite quickly.

How to Request a 3 Month Supply Through Zapmed

If you would prefer to collect several months of contraception at once, the best place to start is with your prescribing doctor.

At Zapmed, you can discuss your contraceptive needs with one of our doctors during your consultation. If it is medically appropriate, the doctor may prescribe your contraception for a longer period or include sufficient repeats on the prescription.

The prescription itself will indicate the approved medication and the intended dispensing structure.

Once you receive your prescription, you can then speak directly with your pharmacy about collecting the full quantity upfront.

It helps to clearly explain that you would like a three month supply if possible. In many cases, pharmacies are able to accommodate this request when:

  • The prescription allows for it
  • The medication is in stock
  • There are no medical or dispensing concerns

If the pharmacy cannot issue the full quantity immediately, they can usually explain the reason and advise what alternatives are available.

The goal is always safe, consistent access to your medication while keeping the process practical and manageable for your everyday life.

If you have questions about contraception, repeat prescriptions, or medication refills, your doctors can help guide you through the process with advice and supportive care.

posts.title: What Zapmed treats (and what we don't)
posts.excerpt: Being able to speak to a medical professional from your own home, at a time that suits you, without sitting in a waiting room or taking half a day off work is the heart of what telehealth offers.
posts.body:
Being able to speak to a medical professional from your own home, at a time that suits you, without sitting in a waiting room or taking half a day off work is the heart of what telehealth offers. And it is exactly what we have built Zapmed around. 

We cover a range of health concerns, handling everything from ongoing prescriptions to new consultations across several areas of care.

That said, we want to be upfront with you about where our scope ends. Some health matters require highly specialised, in-person assessment that a digital platform simply cannot replicate safely. 

Others fall into a category we are legally and ethically required to refer elsewhere, specifically anything that could carry serious or life-threatening risks. 

We take both of these boundaries seriously, not because we want to turn anyone away, but because your safety always comes first.

One of the questions that came through recently was this:

I want to find out if I can chat to a dermatologist for intimate area skin issues.

It is exactly the kind of query we appreciate receiving, and it is far from the only one. Our inbox is full of thoughtful, sometimes uncertain, often brave questions from people just trying to figure out whether we can help. We want more of them. Please keep asking. There is no such thing as a question too awkward or too niche to send our way.

Now, to the question at hand.

Can You Speak to a Dermatologist Through Zapmed About Skin Concerns in Private Areas?

The honest answer is: it depends on what you are dealing with.

Zapmed does have the ability to support patients with certain sexually transmitted infections that present symptoms in or around the genital area. If you are concerned about something you have noticed down there and you suspect it could be an STI, offering appropriate treatment is very much within what we can do for you.

Where things get more complicated is with other types of skin concerns in that region. Conditions involving inflammation, suspected allergic responses, or skin infections affecting the intimate area are not something we are currently set up to assess or treat through our platform. 

These often require visual examination in person, and in some cases laboratory testing or specialist referral, to be diagnosed accurately and safely. Attempting to manage them remotely without that level of assessment would not be doing right by you, and that is not how we operate.

If you are not sure which category your concern falls into, send us a message anyway. We would rather help you figure that out than have you sit with the uncertainty.

What Does Zapmed Offer?

Here is a full picture of the Zapmed services you can access online. 

Contraception

We can prescribe oral contraceptives and can help you find the right option for your body, lifestyle, and health history. Whether you are starting for the first time or looking to switch, our doctors are here to walk you through it.

Sexually Transmitted Infections

From assessment through to prescription, we handle STI consultations with complete discretion and no judgement. Your comfort and confidentiality matter to us enormously.

Erectile Dysfunction

This is one of the most common reasons men reach out to us, and also one of the most underreported. We offer private, supportive consultations and access to effective treatments so that you do not have to navigate this alone.

Hair Loss

Whether you are just starting to notice thinning or have been managing it for a while, we offer treatment options backed by solid medical evidence and personalised to your situation.

Premature Ejaculation

Another area where many people suffer in silence far longer than they need to. Our doctors approach this with sensitivity, and there are real solutions available.

Acne

From mild breakouts to more persistent, stubborn acne, we assess what is going on with your skin and prescribe accordingly, adjusting treatment as your skin responds.

Weight Management

Sometimes you just need to talk to a doctor. Whether it is about a symptom you are worried about, a medication query, or something you have been putting off addressing, we are here for those conversations too.

General GP Consultations

Not everything needs a specialist. For general health concerns, sick certificates, repeat prescriptions, and everyday medical queries, our GPs are here for a proper, attentive consultation.

What We Cannot Treat

There is a category of conditions that telehealth providers are not allowed, or are very limited, in treating conditions that require:

  • a physical examination
  • emergency intervention
  • imaging or lab tests done immediately
  • procedures or surgery
  • high-risk controlled substances

Common examples include:

  • Heart attack symptoms (chest pain, severe shortness of breath)
  • Stroke symptoms (sudden weakness, facial droop, confusion)
  • Severe injuries or heavy bleeding
  • Suspected appendicitis or acute abdominal emergencies
  • Severe allergic reactions/anaphylaxis
  • Psychosis or immediate suicide risk
  • Certain pregnancy emergencies
  • Broken bones needing imaging/casting
  • Conditions requiring hands-on neurological exams
  • Advanced infections needing IV antibiotics or hospitalisation

READ NEXT: How to Prepare for Your First Online Doctor Consultation in South Africa

We May Point You Toward Testing

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can do is not prescribe something but guide you toward the right next step. If you come to us with a concern and, after speaking with one of our doctors, it becomes clear that you would benefit from laboratory testing, imaging, or an in-person review before any treatment is considered, we will tell you that clearly and help you understand where to go.

This is not us turning you away. It is us making sure that whatever happens next is actually right for your health. Getting a proper diagnosis before treatment is always going to serve you better than a guess, however well-intentioned.

You can always come back to us once you have those results, and we will take it from there together.

If you are not sure whether Zapmed is the right fit for what you are going through, feel free to reach out via our website chatbot or social media channels. We would much rather have that conversation with you than have you go without the support you need.

If you previously relied on the medical expertise at Contro, we want to start by reassuring you that the high standard of clinical care you value remains our top priority.

“I previously held an account with Contro. Am I able to simply resume my previous treatment plan, or do I need to begin the entire journey from the beginning?”

Can Former Contro Patients Pick Up Where They Left Off, or Does the Process Have to Be Restarted from Scratch?

The short answer is that you will need to create a new account with Zapmed. We know that’s not the answer everyone was hoping for, but we want to be transparent about why.

Zapmed operates with a team of doctors who are new to your medical history. For them to provide you with safe, appropriate and personalised care, they need to properly assess your health from the ground up. 

Your well-being depends on your treating doctor having a complete and accurate picture of where you are health-wise, and that picture can only be built through a proper consultation. Skipping that step, even for a returning patient, would not be in your best interest.

The reassuring part is that the registration process is very familiar. If you’ve signed up for Contro before, you’ll find that the steps are largely the same. It won’t feel like starting over so much as stepping through a door you’ve walked through before.

Why We Require You to Register Again

Zapmed is a new beginning, and with that comes a new care relationship. Our team of doctors is different from those you may have consulted with previously, and any meaningful medical relationship has to start on solid ground. Your new doctor needs to understand who you are, what your health looks like today, and what you’re hoping to achieve through your care with us. That’s not something we’re able to assume or carry over from a previous provider.

There’s also a medical reason that matters just as much. Your health doesn’t stay static. Even if it’s only been a few months since your last Contro consultation, things may have shifted. Your circumstances, your symptoms, your lifestyle, or even the medication that was previously suitable for you could all look different now. Prescribing any treatment without a current, thorough understanding of your health would not meet the standard of care we hold ourselves to.

A new consultation isn’t a formality. It’s how we make sure that whatever we recommend is right for you at this point in time, not based on a snapshot from months ago. We take that responsibility seriously.

How to Access Zapmed’s Services

Getting started with Zapmed is a simple three-step process.

Step 1: Register a new account

Head to the Zapmed platform and create your account. You’ll provide some basic personal and medical information to help our team understand your background before your consultation.

Step 2: Complete a health questionnaire

You’ll be asked to fill out a health questionnaire covering your current symptoms, medical history, and any treatments you’ve tried before. This helps your doctor prepare for your consultation and ensures your appointment time is spent productively.

Step 3: Select your service and book your first consultation

Choose the service that applies to your health needs and schedule your first appointment with one of our licensed doctors.

From there, the experience mirrors what you may already know. Consultations take place via telehealth, so there’s no need to travel or sit in a waiting room. If treatment is appropriate following your consultation, our doctor will issue a prescription, which is sent directly to our partner pharmacy. They will prepare your medication and arrange delivery to your door.

The model is the same. The convenience is the same. The care is the same.
